stimulus.title: The Night Shift of the Brain
stimulus.text: Sleep can look like idleness, but the brain is busy. During deep sleep, waves of electrical activity sweep across the cortex, and researchers think these waves help move the day's memories into longer-term storage. In one line of experiments, students who slept after studying a list of words remembered more of them than students who stayed awake the same number of hours. Sleep may also clear away molecular waste that builds up while we are awake. None of this means more sleep is always better; the relationship appears to follow a curve, with both too little and too much linked to poorer performance. What the brain seems to need is enough, at the right times.

stimulus.title: Bubbles of Old Air
stimulus.text: Each winter's snowfall on a polar ice sheet does not entirely melt; it packs down, traps tiny pockets of air, and slowly turns to ice. Layer settles on layer, year after year, so that drilling deep into the ice is a way of drilling back through time. Trapped in those bubbles is a sample of the very atmosphere that existed when the snow fell, including the gases it carried. By analyzing cores pulled from kilometers down, researchers can compare today's air with the air of tens of thousands of years ago. The ice keeps no diary of dates, yet its layers, counted carefully, let scientists assign an age to each whisper of ancient air.

stimulus.title: Forty Moves
stimulus.text: By the thirtieth move, Priya had stopped seeing the pieces as pieces. The knight on the rim was a trapped thing with one way out; the pawn on the sixth rank was a promise she had made twenty moves earlier and now had to keep. Across the table her opponent, a boy in a sweatshirt who had not looked up once, took her bishop with an unhurried hand and pressed the clock. Nine minutes left for her, fourteen for him. Her coach's voice surfaced: when you are behind on time, do not think faster; think about fewer things. She let the whole board blur except for the pawn and the two squares in front of it. There was a path. It required giving up the knight, which her hand did not want to do, and she noticed, with something like amusement, that her hand had opinions. She moved the knight anyway. The boy looked up.

stimulus.title: A Letter from the Camp
stimulus.text: Dear Margaret, You will forgive the hand; I am writing on the lid of a trunk by the light of a lamp that smokes. We reached the river camp on Tuesday, two days later than the captain promised and a full week later than Father feared, which puts the truth, as usual, somewhere between hope and worry. The country here is nothing like the engravings. The hills are brown and lie about in heaps, and the river is the color of weak coffee. I had expected to be lonely and find instead that I am never alone, which is worse. There are forty of us in a space meant for twenty. Still, this morning a boy no older than you showed me how to find water by watching where the birds go at dusk, and I thought: here is something I would not have learned at home. Tell Mother I am eating. It is nearly true. Your brother, Thomas.

stimulus.title: The Lamp Room
stimulus.text: Every evening at dusk, Ines climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps to the lamp room, counting them under her breath as her father had taught her. He was ill that winter, and the keeper's log, which he had kept in his cramped, careful hand for twenty years, now bore her looser script. She trimmed the wick, polished the great lens until her own face swam in it, and set the clockwork turning. Below, the sea worried at the rocks. Ines did not love the lighthouse, exactly; she loved the moment when the beam first swung out across the water and she imagined a ship's mate, miles off, lifting his head. It was the only conversation she had ever had with strangers, and it consisted of a single word, repeated all night: here.

stimulus.title: The Eleven-Forty
stimulus.text: The station at Harwell had two platforms and one clock, and the clock was wrong, which everyone in town knew and no one corrected. Mrs. Abernathy stood under it in her good coat with a hatbox at her feet. She had told her sister she was going to visit a cousin in the city for a fortnight. The cousin existed; the fortnight did not. In her handbag, beneath the gloves, was a letter from a music conservatory addressed to a Miss E. Abernathy, which she had not been for twelve years, and which she had opened at the kitchen table that morning while the kettle screamed and nobody came to take it off. The eleven-forty was late. It was always late, by exactly the amount the clock was wrong, so that it arrived, in a manner of speaking, on time. She picked up the hatbox when she heard it. She had not yet decided whether she would get on.

stimulus.title: In Defense of Doing Nothing
stimulus.text: We have made an idol of productivity. Every hour is to be optimized, every habit tracked, every pause justified as 'recharging' for the work to come. Even rest is permitted only as an investment. I want to argue for something less respectable: time that is not for anything. The case is not sentimental. Most people can name the moment a stubborn problem came loose, and it was rarely at the desk. It was in the shower, on a walk, in the dull middle of a long drive. The mind does its deepest sorting when it is left alone, and it cannot be left alone on a schedule. A culture that fills every gap does not merely tire its members; it starves the very faculty it claims to prize. I do not propose that anyone work less. I propose that when the work is done, we stop pretending that the hours afterward owe us a return. Some of them will pay anyway. That is not why they are worth having.

stimulus.title: The Unfinished Coast
stimulus.text: My master, Mr. Hallam, had drawn maps for the Admiralty for thirty years, and in all that time, he told me, he had never once drawn a line he had not been given reason to believe. I was nineteen and thought this a modest ambition. It was my task that winter to copy the surveys sent back from the northern voyage, and I came to a stretch of coast where the ship's log simply stopped: fog for nine days, then open sea. The chart before me showed a gap. I proposed to close it with a gentle curve, as any sensible coast would run. Mr. Hallam took the pen from my hand. 'A sailor who trusts that curve,' he said, 'will put his ship on rocks we have not seen, and he will do it in the dark, and he will do it because you were tidy.' He left the gap. I have since drawn a great many maps, and some of them have gaps, and I have come to think of the gaps as the most honest lines on them.

stimulus.title: What Is Ours
stimulus.text: I used to keep a list of things that had gone wrong that week, with the idea that reviewing it would make me wiser. It made me miserable instead, and I eventually understood why. Most of the items were not mine. The weather, a colleague's mood, the outcome of a vote in a city I had never visited: I had been grading myself on events in which I had no vote. An ancient school of philosophers drew a line that I have since found useful. On one side are the things within our power—our judgments, our efforts, our intentions. On the other side is everything else. They did not say that the second category is unimportant, only that it is not ours, and that confusing the two is the chief source of unhappiness. I still keep a list. It is shorter now, and every item on it is something I actually did, or failed to do. On bad weeks it is a harder list to read. On good weeks it is the only one that counts.

stimulus.title: Division
stimulus.text: 'You take the clock,' Dana said. 'You always liked it.' 'I never liked it,' said Ben. 'I wound it because nobody else would.' They were sitting on the floor of their mother's apartment with the lists between them, hers typed, his on the back of an envelope. It was the fourth hour. They had agreed easily on the furniture, which neither wanted, and the photographs, which they would scan and share, and had come, as they had both known they would, to the small things: the clock, the chipped blue bowl, the cheap ring their mother had worn in place of the good one she kept in a drawer. 'Then I'll take it,' Dana said, and wrote it down, and Ben watched her write and felt, absurdly, that something had been taken from him. 'Or we could sell it,' she said, not looking up. 'No,' he said, too quickly, and they both heard it. She crossed it off her list. He picked up the clock. It was heavier than he remembered.

stimulus.title: Noon by Agreement
stimulus.text: Until the 1880s, noon in most American towns was simply the moment the sun stood highest over that town. A traveler heading west from one city to the next could find the clocks a few minutes behind at each stop, and nobody minded, because few people traveled fast enough to notice. The railroads changed this. A train running on a timetable built from dozens of local noons was a train waiting to collide with another. In 1883, the major rail companies divided the continent into four broad zones and declared that every clock within a zone would read the same. The federal government did not endorse the scheme for another thirty-five years, and some towns refused outright, keeping 'sun time' as a point of pride. But commerce followed the trains. Within a few years, most people had quietly agreed to let a company's timetable, rather than the sky, tell them what time it was.

stimulus.title: Learning Late
stimulus.text: I learned to swim at thirty-four, in a municipal pool that smelled of chlorine and other people's shampoo, in a class otherwise made up of children. The instructor, a patient woman named Rosa, treated me exactly as she treated the eight-year-olds, which I resented for one lesson and was grateful for ever after. Children, it turns out, are not afraid of the water in the way adults are. They are afraid of it the way they are afraid of the dark: thoroughly, and without any theory about it. I had theories. I knew about buoyancy and breath control and the physics of floating, and all of it deserted me the moment my feet left the bottom. What Rosa taught me, in the end, was not a technique but a sequence of permissions. You may put your face in. You may let go of the wall. You may trust that the water, which does not care about you, will nevertheless hold you up. By the fourth week I could cross the pool. By the eighth I had stopped counting.

stimulus.title: Blood That Will Not Freeze
stimulus.text: The waters around Antarctica hover just below the freezing point of fresh water all year, kept liquid only by their salt. A fish's blood is less salty than the sea, so by rights the fish that live there should freeze solid from the inside. They do not, and the reason is a family of proteins unlike anything in warm-water species. These antifreeze proteins do not lower the freezing point of blood the way salt does. Instead they attach to the faces of any ice crystal that begins to form and stop it from growing, so that the crystal stays microscopic and harmless. The strategy is cheap: a small amount of protein guards an enormous volume of blood. Genetic comparisons suggest the proteins arose from a digestive enzyme whose gene was copied and gradually altered over millions of years. The fish did not invent a new molecule from nothing. It repurposed an old one, which is how evolution usually proceeds.

stimulus.title: What She Planted
stimulus.text: My grandmother's fig tree should not have survived a single winter in our city. Every November she wrapped it in burlap and old blankets and tied the bundle with twine, so that for four months the backyard held what looked like a mummy standing guard over the frozen tomato beds. The neighbors found this eccentric. I found it embarrassing, in the way that everything about her was embarrassing to me at fourteen: the accent, the plastic bags folded and saved, the way she called across the yard to me in a language I answered in English. The figs came in August. They were small and purple and split at the bottom when ripe, and she would not let anyone else pick them. The summer after she died, I unwrapped the tree myself and found I had been watching her more carefully than I knew: I remembered the order of the knots. The tree bore that year. I ate the first fig standing in the yard, and I did not call anyone.

stimulus.title: The Translator's Choice
stimulus.text: Readers often assume that a good translation is a transparent one, a pane of glass through which the original can be seen undistorted. The assumption is flattering to translators and entirely false. Every language carves the world differently. A word that is ordinary in one tongue may have no single equivalent in another, only a cluster of near-misses, each of which drags in connotations the author never intended. The translator must choose, and every choice is a small act of authorship. Consider a poem whose rhythm depends on short, blunt words. Rendered into a language whose common words run to four syllables, it can keep its meaning or keep its music, but rarely both. Some translators preserve the sense and let the poem go slack; others invent new images to save the beat. Neither is wrong, and neither is the original. The honest translator does not pretend to be a window. She admits to being a second author, and asks to be judged as one.

stimulus.title: More Than Books
stimulus.text: Whenever a city faces a budget shortfall, someone proposes cutting the library. The reasoning is familiar: books are cheap, the internet is everywhere, and surely a building full of shelves is a luxury. This reasoning misunderstands what a library now does. In most cities the library is the only indoor public space where no one is required to buy anything. It is where people without a home address receive mail, where job seekers print résumés, where children whose parents work late are safe until dinner, and where someone learning a new language can practice without embarrassment. None of these services appears in a count of books checked out, which is why library budgets look so easy to trim. A city that closes its library does not save the cost of the services the library provided. It simply transfers that cost, in a less visible form, to its emergency rooms, its police, and its schools.

stimulus.title: Dancing Directions
stimulus.text: When a honeybee forager returns to the hive after finding a rich patch of flowers, she does not simply hand over nectar and leave. She performs a dance on the vertical face of the comb, running forward in a straight line while shaking her abdomen, then circling back to repeat the run. Decades of experiments have shown that the dance is a map. The angle of the run relative to straight up corresponds to the angle of the food relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggling encodes distance: roughly one second of waggling for every kilometer. Other bees crowd around, touch the dancer with their antennae, and later fly out in the direction described. The system is imperfect; recruits often land a hundred meters off target. But a forager who dances for a good site sends many sisters toward it, and small errors are corrected when those sisters return and dance themselves.

stimulus.title: The Same Ship
stimulus.text: An old puzzle asks us to imagine a wooden ship whose planks are replaced one at a time as they rot, until not a single original board remains. Is it still the same ship? Most people say yes; a ship is not its planks but a pattern that persists through them. Now suppose someone collected every discarded plank and reassembled them in a warehouse. Which vessel is the original: the one that sailed continuously, or the one built from the original wood? The puzzle is not really about ships. It asks what makes anything the same thing over time, including a person whose cells, memories, and opinions turn over across decades. One tempting answer is that identity is a matter of continuity rather than of material: the ship that kept sailing, and the person who kept living, carry their history forward even as their substance is exchanged. Whether that answer is correct, it at least explains why the warehouse ship feels like an imposter.

stimulus.title: The Otter's Shadow
stimulus.text: Along parts of the northern Pacific coast, forests of kelp rise thirty meters from the seafloor, sheltering fish, crabs, and the young of many open-water species. In the twentieth century, some of these forests vanished, leaving stretches of bare rock that ecologists called urchin barrens. The cause was not pollution or warming water but the absence of a single predator. Sea otters, hunted nearly to extinction for their fur, had once eaten enormous quantities of sea urchins. Without otters, urchin populations exploded, and the urchins, which graze on kelp, mowed the forests down. Where otters were later reintroduced, the sequence ran in reverse: urchins declined, kelp recovered, and within a decade fish returned. The otter is what ecologists call a keystone species, an organism whose influence on its ecosystem is far larger than its numbers would suggest. Remove the keystone and the arch does not weaken gradually. It falls.

stimulus.title: Answering the Horn
stimulus.text: A visitor to a jazz club for the first time may wonder how a band with no sheet music avoids chaos. Part of the answer is a structure older than jazz itself. In call and response, one voice makes a statement and another answers it, as a preacher's line is answered by a congregation or a field song by a chorus. Jazz musicians absorbed this pattern and made it the grammar of improvisation. A trumpet plays a phrase; the saxophone replies, perhaps repeating the phrase, perhaps mocking it, perhaps turning it upside down. The drummer, hearing both, answers with an accent that comments on the exchange. Nothing is written down because nothing needs to be. Each player is bound to listen, since the rules of the form make a reply to what was just played the only acceptable move. What sounds to the newcomer like freedom is in fact a conversation, with the same obligations any conversation carries: to attend, to respond, and to leave room.

stimulus.title: Seven Years of Silence
stimulus.text: In the workshops of medieval European towns, a boy of twelve might be bound to a master craftsman for seven years. The contract, signed by his parents, obliged the master to feed, house, and teach him and obliged the boy to obey, keep the trade's secrets, and accept no wages. To modern eyes the arrangement looks exploitative, and sometimes it was. But the guilds that oversaw these contracts had reasons that went beyond cheap labor. A trade such as glassmaking or dyeing depended on knowledge that was never written down, partly because it could not be: how long to hold a rod in the furnace, how a vat should smell when the color is ready. Such knowledge passed only through years of watching and failing. The long term also protected the town. A half-trained craftsman who set up shop could ruin the reputation of a whole trade. Seven years was the guild's guarantee to its customers that anyone selling under its name had earned the right.

stimulus.title: First on the Stone
stimulus.text: On a fresh lava flow or a boulder newly exposed by a retreating glacier, the first living thing to arrive is usually something most people would not notice: a gray or orange crust, flat as paint, called a lichen. A lichen is not one organism but two. A fungus provides the structure and anchors itself to bare rock; algae living inside it carry out photosynthesis and supply sugars to both. Neither partner could survive alone on stone, but together they can live where there is no soil at all. Over decades the lichen secretes weak acids that etch the rock surface, and its own dead layers mix with windblown dust to form the first thin smear of soil. Mosses follow, then grasses, then shrubs whose roots pry the rock apart further. The lichen is long gone by the time trees arrive, shaded out by the forest it made possible. Ecologists call it a pioneer species, and like many pioneers it does not get to enjoy what it built.

stimulus.title: Measuring the Night
stimulus.text: Complaints about city noise are easy to collect and hard to interpret, since the people who complain are rarely a representative sample. A team of researchers therefore took a different approach. They lent wrist monitors to 412 residents of a mid-sized city, placed sound meters in each bedroom, and recorded both for three weeks. The results were less tidy than headlines about 'noisy cities' suggest. Average nightly noise explained only a small share of the variation in sleep quality. What mattered far more was the number of sudden peaks—a siren, a slammed door, a motorcycle—above the background hum. Residents who experienced more than eight such peaks per night slept, on average, forty minutes less than those with fewer than three, even when their average noise levels were nearly identical. The finding suggests that policies aimed at lowering a neighborhood's overall decibel level may be targeting the wrong number.

stimulus.title: The Moon's Hidden Side
stimulus.text: No one on Earth had seen the far side of the Moon until a spacecraft photographed it in 1959, and the reason is not that the Moon fails to rotate. It rotates exactly once for every orbit it completes, so that the same hemisphere always faces us. This coincidence is not a coincidence. Early in its history the Moon spun faster, but Earth's gravity raised a slight bulge in its body, and that bulge, dragged along by the Moon's rotation, was pulled back by Earth's gravity in a way that acted as a brake. Over hundreds of millions of years the spin slowed until the bulge pointed steadily at Earth and the braking stopped. Astronomers call the result tidal locking, and it is common: most large moons in the solar system show one face to their planets. Earth is subject to the same effect from the Moon. Our days are lengthening by about two milliseconds per century, which is why the Moon, patient as it is, has not yet managed to lock us.

stimulus.title: The Cold Sleep
stimulus.text: A hummingbird burns energy faster, for its size, than almost any other vertebrate. Its heart can beat more than a thousand times a minute, and it must feed every few minutes during the day simply to stay alive. Night poses an obvious problem: twelve hours without nectar would exhaust a bird that weighs less than a coin. The solution is a state called torpor. As darkness falls, the bird's body temperature drops by twenty degrees or more, its heart slows to a few dozen beats a minute, and its breathing becomes so faint that early naturalists sometimes mistook torpid hummingbirds for dead ones. Energy use falls by as much as ninety percent. Torpor is not without cost. A bird in deep torpor cannot flee a predator, and warming back up at dawn takes time and energy of its own. Hummingbirds therefore seem to use the state judiciously, sinking deepest on cold nights or when their fat reserves are low, and staying nearer to wakefulness when they can afford to.

stimulus.title: Counting the Reef
stimulus.text: A coral reef looks like rock, but it is a city of animals, each polyp hosting algae that feed it through photosynthesis and lend it color. When water grows too warm, the polyps expel their algae and turn ghostly white, a process called bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. Surveys of one large reef system tracked the share of coral cover that bleached during three heat events. In the first, water temperatures exceeded the local summer maximum by one degree Celsius for four weeks, and about 30 percent of surveyed colonies bleached. In the second, the same excess lasted eight weeks, and bleaching rose to roughly 60 percent. In the third, a two-degree excess for four weeks produced bleaching comparable to the second event. The pattern suggests that what harms coral is not temperature alone but accumulated heat—how far above normal, multiplied by how long. Reefs that recovered fully did so only when more than a decade passed between events.

stimulus.title: Stones Out of Place
stimulus.text: Travelers across the farmland of the northern plains sometimes notice a boulder the size of a cart sitting alone in a field, miles from any rock of its kind. Farmers once called such stones 'erratics,' and the name was apt: nothing in the surrounding geology could explain how they got there. The explanation lay to the north. During the last ice age, sheets of ice more than a kilometer thick crept south, plucking rock from the bedrock beneath and carrying it, frozen in place, for hundreds of kilometers. When the climate warmed and the ice melted, everything it carried dropped where it stood. The ridges of gravel that mark the farthest advance of the ice, called moraines, now run across the landscape like the rim of a dried puddle. By matching an erratic's minerals to the bedrock where they originate, geologists can trace the path of ice that vanished ten thousand years ago, reading a map drawn by something that no longer exists.

stimulus.title: Scrubbing the Centuries
stimulus.text: When restorers cleaned a famous ceiling fresco in the 1980s, removing five hundred years of soot, candle smoke, and old varnish, they revealed colors so bright that some critics refused to believe them. The pale blues and acid greens, the critics argued, could not be the painter's own; the cleaning must have stripped away a final layer of shading the artist had applied by hand. The restorers answered that the dark layer was glue, applied by earlier restorers to revive a surface dulled by smoke, and that the chemistry of the residue supported their account. The dispute was never fully settled, and perhaps it could not be. Every cleaning is a wager about which layers are the work and which are the damage. The restorers wagered that the painter wanted brilliance; the critics wagered that he wanted depth. Both sides claimed to speak for an artist who had been dead for four centuries and who, inconveniently, had left no instructions.

stimulus.title: The Logic of the Line
stimulus.text: A line is a strange institution. No law requires a crowd at a bus stop to arrange itself in order of arrival, and no one is paid to enforce the arrangement; yet in many places the line forms anyway, and someone who cuts in provokes a resentment far out of proportion to the few seconds lost. Economists who study such norms point out that the line solves a problem that would otherwise be solved by pushing, and that everyone in it, including the person at the back, benefits from a rule that keeps the strong from simply going first. Field studies reveal a subtler pattern. People will tolerate a cutter who offers a reason, even a flimsy one, far more readily than one who offers none, and they will defend the place of a stranger ahead of them almost as fiercely as their own. The line, in other words, is less a queue of individuals than a small, temporary society with a shared sense of what is owed.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Grades, the author argues, are a poor measure of learning and a worse motivator. Students taught to chase a letter learn to ask what will be on the test rather than what is true, and they abandon a subject the moment the grade is secured. Schools that have replaced grades with written feedback report students taking harder courses, asking more questions, and revising work they would once have discarded. The letter grade compresses a semester of thinking into a single symbol that tells a student almost nothing about what to do next. Feedback tells them exactly that, and does so while there is still time to act on it.
stimulus.text_b: Written feedback is valuable, this author agrees, and no one defends a grade as a complete account of a student. But grades do work that feedback cannot. They are comparable across teachers and schools, which lets a college or employer read a transcript from a school it has never heard of. They make it harder for bias to hide, since a vague paragraph can flatter one student and damn another without ever stating a standard. And for many students, a clear target is not a corruption of learning but the thing that gets them to the desk at all. The right reform is to improve grades, not to abolish them.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Using recovered genetic material to bring back vanished species, the author argues, is the most hopeful project in modern biology. A herd of cold-adapted elephants grazing the northern tundra could help restore grasslands that once held carbon in their soils, and the techniques developed along the way, from gene editing to artificial wombs, would serve the conservation of species that are endangered now. Extinction has always been treated as a final verdict. For the first time, it might become an appeal. The author acknowledges the project is expensive but sees in it something the field has lacked for decades: a reason for optimism.
stimulus.text_b: Resurrecting a mammoth, this author contends, would produce not a mammoth but an elephant with a few mammoth genes, raised without the mother, the herd, or the climate that made the original what it was. The money, measured in hundreds of millions, would protect dozens of species that are vanishing today and need only habitat and enforcement rather than invention. The author worries most about the lesson. If the public comes to believe that extinction is reversible, the urgency that drives conservation drains away. Hope is valuable. False hope, the author warns, is worse than none.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Companies that have tried a four-day week without cutting pay, the author reports, have mostly kept it. Employees, given a day back, cut the meetings and idle hours that had filled the fifth, and output in trials across several countries held steady while sick days fell and resignations dropped by more than a third. The author argues that the five-day week was never a law of nature; it was a compromise struck a century ago for factory labor, and knowledge work has simply inherited it. A schedule that produces the same work with less exhaustion is not a perk, the text concludes. It is the correction of a mistake.
stimulus.text_b: The four-day trials are encouraging, this author allows, but they share a flaw: the companies that volunteer for them are the ones most likely to succeed. They are small, office-based, and already flexible. A hospital, a school, or a restaurant cannot compress a week; it can only hire more people, which the trials' accounting never includes. Even in offices, the author notes, the gains came partly from cutting work that was wasteful in the first place, which a firm could do on any schedule. The text does not oppose shorter weeks. It warns that a result from firms that chose to be studied cannot be assumed to hold for firms that did not.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Banning thin plastic grocery bags, the author argues, is one of the rare environmental policies that costs almost nothing and works. Within a year of one city's ban, the number of plastic bags found in storm drains and along the shoreline fell by roughly half, and shoppers adapted within weeks, as they had been told they would not. The bag itself was never essential; it was a convenience that had become a habit, and habits can be changed by a small, well-timed push. The author sees the ban as a model: pick the waste that is most visible, most avoidable, and least missed.
stimulus.text_b: The bans do reduce litter, this author agrees, but their effect on the environment as a whole is less clear. When thin bags disappear, shoppers buy thicker plastic bags for trash cans and pet waste, and many of the reusable bags handed out in their place are made of materials that require dozens of uses before they outperform the bag they replaced. Studies in several cities find total plastic consumption falling by far less than the bag count suggests. The author does not call for repealing the bans. The point is that a visible result is not the same as a large one, and that policy should be judged by the second.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Raising the minimum age for social media accounts to sixteen, the author argues, is the least a society can do for its adolescents. A ban would push younger users onto platforms with no safety features at all, since enforcement by birthdate is trivially evaded. The author favors stricter design rules, such as limits on notifications and infinite scrolling, that would apply to every user. Fix the product, the text argues, rather than fencing off the people.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Requiring students to memorize poems, the author argues, is not an antique practice but a gift. A poem carried in memory is available anywhere: on a bus, in a hospital waiting room, at a graveside. Students who learn lines by heart come to feel the rhythm of the language from the inside, in a way that reading silently never provides, and they acquire a store of phrases that will shape how they write and speak for the rest of their lives. The objection that memorization is mere rote misses the point. One does not memorize a poem instead of understanding it. One memorizes it in order to understand it slowly, over years.
stimulus.text_b: Memorization has its pleasures, this author grants, but classroom time is scarce and should go where it does the most good. An hour spent drilling lines is an hour not spent discussing what a poem means, comparing it with another, or writing in response to it. The students who thrive at recitation are often those who already love the material; for the rest, the assignment confirms a suspicion that poetry is a performance of obedience. If the goal is a lifelong relationship with poems, the author suggests, it is better served by teaching students how to find and read new ones than by fixing a few old ones in their heads.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Students who take notes by hand, the author reports, consistently remember more of a lecture than those who type. Because writing is slower, they cannot transcribe, so they must decide what matters and put it in their own words, and that act of compression is itself a form of learning. Typists, by contrast, tend to produce near-verbatim records that they never fully process. In several experiments, the handwriting advantage held even when typists were explicitly warned not to transcribe. The author concludes that the pen's limitations are a feature, and recommends that lecture halls discourage laptops.
stimulus.text_b: The author accepts the finding that handwriting aids memory in the lecture hall but questions the recommendation that follows. The experiments measured recall of a single lecture within a week. They did not measure what students did afterward with their notes, and typed notes are far easier to search, reorganize, and share when preparing for an exam weeks later. Nor did the studies include students with disabilities, for whom a keyboard may be the only practical option. Rather than banning laptops, the author suggests teaching students to type the way good note-takers write: selectively, in their own words, and with the lecture rather than the screen as the focus.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Supporters of remote work point to a decade of surveys in which employees report doing more in fewer hours when they work from home. The savings are not mysterious: no commute, fewer interruptions, and the freedom to schedule deep work when one's attention is sharpest. Companies that measured output rather than hours, the author notes, found that productivity held steady or rose when offices closed, while turnover fell. The office, on this view, was never where the work got done; it was where the work got watched. A firm that insists on attendance is paying for supervision it does not need and losing workers who can find flexibility elsewhere.
stimulus.text_b: The productivity gains reported by remote workers are real but misleading, this author argues, because they measure the wrong period. In the first year of working from home, employees drew on relationships and shared knowledge built over years in the office. The question is what happens when that stock runs down. Studies tracking new hires who never met their colleagues in person find slower skill growth and weaker ties to the people who could help them. Individual output may hold up; the collective capacity to train, mentor, and improvise together erodes quietly. The office, the author concludes, was less a place of supervision than a place of apprenticeship.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Spending billions to send people to other worlds while problems remain unsolved at home, the author argues, reflects misplaced priorities. The money devoted to a single crewed mission could fund clean water for millions or research into diseases that kill every year. Robots, moreover, can collect most of the scientific data humans could, at a fraction of the cost and risk. The romance of exploration is real, but romance is a poor basis for budgets. A government's first obligation is to the people who already live on the planet it governs, and every launch should be weighed against what the same money could do for them.
stimulus.text_b: The author does not dispute that needs on Earth are urgent, but argues that framing the choice as exploration versus welfare is false. Space budgets are a small fraction of national spending, far smaller than most people guess, and cutting them would not transfer the savings to clean water; it would simply reduce them. Meanwhile, the engineering required to keep humans alive in hostile environments has produced water purification, medical monitoring, and weather forecasting that serve people who will never leave Earth. The question, the text suggests, is not whether to look up or down, but whether we can do both well.

stimulus.title: Battery Voltage Over Time
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students connected a fresh AA battery to a small lamp and measured the battery's voltage with a voltmeter at regular intervals while the lamp stayed on.
Results (the voltage of the battery): at 0 h, 1.61 V; at 2 h, 1.54 V; at 4 h, 1.42 V; at 6 h, 1.27 V; at 8 h, 1.08 V.

questions.prompt: Why did the experimenters most likely time 10 complete swings and divide by 10 rather than time a single swing in Experiment 1?

choices.text: Remove the need to keep the angle from which the bob was released the same
choices.rationale: Repetition does not substitute for controlling variables; controls are still needed.

choices.text: Make the period of the pendulum change more in response to string length

choices.text: Reduce the effect of random error in individual measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging repeated measurements cancels out much of the random variation in any single measurement.

questions.explanation: Any single measurement contains random error; repeating and averaging makes the recorded value more reliable.

stimulus.title: Pendulum Period
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students hung a metal bob from a string, pulled the bob 10° to one side, and released it. They timed 10 complete swings with a stopwatch and divided by 10 to find the period. The procedure was repeated for several string lengths.
Results (the period of the pendulum): at 20 cm, 0.88 s; at 40 cm, 1.25 s; at 60 cm, 1.53 s; at 80 cm, 1.77 s; at 100 cm, 1.97 s; at 120 cm, 2.16 s.

questions.prompt: Why did the experimenters most likely measure the tread depth at 5 values of distance driven spread across a range, instead of at only the lowest and highest values?

stimulus.title: Distance Driven and Tire Wear
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A testing company fitted new tires of one model to the same car and measured the tread depth with a gauge after each 10,000 km of driving on a fixed route.
Results (the tread depth): at 0 km, 8.9 mm; at 10000 km, 7.9 mm; at 20000 km, 6.8 mm; at 30000 km, 5.8 mm; at 40000 km, 4.7 mm.

questions.prompt: If the experimenters wanted their measurements of the horizontal distance the ball traveled to be more reliable, they should most likely:

choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each launch angle and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

choices.text: Test fewer values of launch angle so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

choices.text: Record the horizontal distance the ball traveled to fewer decimal places to simplify the table
choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

questions.explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

stimulus.title: Launch Angle and Range
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students used a spring launcher to fire the same ball at a set angle above the horizontal, always with the spring compressed by the same amount. They measured the horizontal distance from the launcher to the landing point. Each angle was fired three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the horizontal distance the ball traveled): at 20°, 14.4 m; at 30°, 18.7 m; at 40°, 20.5 m; at 50°, 19.9 m; at 60°, 17.0 m; at 70°, 12.3 m.

stimulus.title: Speed and Stopping Distance

stimulus.title: Slope and Soil Erosion
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students filled identical trays with 5 kg of the same soil, tilted each tray to a set angle, and sprinkled water evenly over it from a watering can. They collected the soil that washed out of the tray, dried it, and found its mass.

stimulus.title: Seed Soaking and Germination
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students soaked batches of 50 radish seeds in water for a set number of hours, then placed each batch on damp paper towels in a covered tray. After 5 days they counted the seeds that had sprouted and converted the count to a percent.

questions.prompt: Suppose the experimenters wanted to test whether the volume of hydrogen peroxide affects the time for the reaction to finish. Which change to the procedure of Experiment 1 would best test this?

choices.text: Measure the volume of hydrogen peroxide in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the time for the reaction to finish

choices.text: Vary the volume of hydrogen peroxide while holding the mass of catalyst and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Vary both the volume of hydrogen peroxide and the mass of catalyst at the same time in each trial, measuring the time for the reaction to finish
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the mass of catalyst
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about catalyst mass but never changes the volume of hydrogen peroxide.

questions.explanation: A fair test of the volume of hydrogen peroxide changes it alone. The mass of catalyst, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

questions.prompt: A student claims that the temperature of the solution affects the time for the reaction to finish. Do the results of Experiments 1 and 2 support this claim?

choices.text: No; the two experiments gave the same reaction time at every catalyst mass tested
choices.rationale: The columns differ at every catalyst mass; compare them row by row.

choices.text: No; the time for the reaction to finish decreased as catalyst mass increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: A shared trend with catalyst mass says nothing about whether the temperature of the solution matters; the two columns differ at every row.

choices.text: Yes; at every catalyst mass tested, the time for the reaction to finish was higher for 20°C than for 30°C
choices.rationale: Correct. The two experiments differ only in this condition, and the results differ consistently between them.

choices.text: Yes; the time for the reaction to finish decreased as catalyst mass increased in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2
choices.rationale: That trend concerns catalyst mass, not the temperature of the solution; it would appear even if the condition had no effect.

questions.explanation: Because the experiments differ only in the temperature of the solution, the consistent gap between the two sets of results (higher for 20°C) shows that the condition affects the time for the reaction to finish.

questions.prompt: To decide whether the type of meal has an effect on the blood glucose level, a student should compare the results of:

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the type of meal
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the time after the meal under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the type of meal, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the time after the meal was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying time in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed consisting of whole-grain bread with the same number of calories
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the type of meal; a comparison is required.

questions.explanation: Each experiment holds the type of meal fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Blood Glucose After a Meal
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A volunteer ate a measured meal consisting of a sugary drink after fasting overnight. A small blood sample was taken at set times afterward and its glucose concentration measured with a glucose meter.
Results (the blood glucose level): at 15 min, 137 mg/dL; at 30 min, 158 mg/dL; at 45 min, 161 mg/dL; at 60 min, 154 mg/dL; at 90 min, 133 mg/dL.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated consisting of whole-grain bread with the same number of calories, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 15 min, 116 mg/dL; at 30 min, 129 mg/dL; at 45 min, 131 mg/dL; at 60 min, 127 mg/dL; at 90 min, 114 mg/dL.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most serious flaw in the procedure of Experiment 1?

stimulus.title: Enzyme Activity and pH

Results (the activity of the enzyme): at pH 3, 4 µmol/min; at pH 4, 19 µmol/min; at pH 5, 44 µmol/min; at pH 6, 51 µmol/min; at pH 7, 29 µmol/min; at pH 8, 8 µmol/min.

stimulus.title: Speed and Fuel Efficiency
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A test driver drove the same car around a flat track at a steady speed with only the driver aboard for 20 km and measured the fuel used. Fuel efficiency was calculated as kilometers traveled per liter of fuel.
Results (the fuel efficiency): at 60 km/h, 16.5 km/L; at 70 km/h, 17.1 km/L; at 80 km/h, 17.2 km/L; at 90 km/h, 16.9 km/L; at 100 km/h, 16.2 km/L.

Experiment 2

stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

questions.prompt: Scientist 1 and Scientist 2 would both most likely agree that:

choices.rationale: Both describe the Moon's core as small.

choices.text: the Moon formed from debris produced by a collision.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 proposes a collision.

choices.text: the Moon's orbit is not tilted relative to Earth's equator.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 states the orbit is tilted; Scientist 1 does not dispute this.

choices.text: the Moon's rocks have oxygen isotope ratios similar to Earth's.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both accept the isotope match and offer different explanations for it.

questions.explanation: The isotope similarity is a shared fact; each scientist explains it differently.

stimulus.title: The Origin of the Moon
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision blasted molten rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it quickly gathered into the Moon. This explains why the Moon's rocks match Earth's in the ratios of oxygen isotopes, which differ from one body to another in the solar system. It also explains why the Moon has a very small iron core: the impact stripped mostly rocky material from the outside of the Earth, leaving Earth's iron core behind. The Moon's rocks are also unusually dry, as expected if they were once heated enough to drive off their water.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was captured by Earth's gravity as it passed nearby. Capture explains why the Moon is so large compared with Earth; the impact scenario should have left a much smaller moon or none at all, as computer models of similar collisions often show. The matching oxygen isotopes could result from the Moon forming in the same region of the solar system as Earth, from the same raw material. A capture would have left the Moon in a tilted orbit, and the Moon's orbit is indeed tilted relative to Earth's equator. The small core could simply reflect the Moon's original composition.

questions.prompt: Suppose each of the following were discovered. Which one would most strengthen Scientist 1's position?

choices.rationale: Carbon dioxide falling first supports Scientist 2's view that it drives the cooling.

choices.text: Climate models show that small changes in sunlight cannot, by themselves, grow large ice sheets.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's objection to the orbital explanation.

choices.text: Ocean circulation is found to change sharply just before each ice age.
choices.rationale: Circulation changes releasing or absorbing carbon dioxide fit Scientist 2's account.

choices.text: Ice ages are found to begin only at minima of northern summer sunlight, whatever the carbon dioxide level.
choices.rationale: Correct. Ice ages tied to sunlight minima independent of carbon dioxide make the orbital cycles the controlling factor.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1 claims sunlight changes control ice ages; a finding that ice ages track sunlight minima regardless of carbon dioxide supports that.

stimulus.title: What Drives the Ice Ages
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Ice ages are driven by slow, regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt. Over tens of thousands of years, the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis, and the direction the axis points all shift in predictable cycles. These cycles change how much summer sunlight reaches the far northern lands. When northern summers are cool, winter snow does not fully melt, ice sheets grow, and their bright surfaces reflect still more sunlight. Records from deep-sea sediments show that the timing of past ice ages matches the periods of the orbital cycles. The cycles are the pacemaker; everything else follows.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Orbital cycles are too weak to produce ice ages on their own. The change in sunlight they cause is small, and it is spread across the year. The real driver is carbon dioxide. Air bubbles trapped in ancient ice show that carbon dioxide levels fell during every ice age and rose during every warm period, and carbon dioxide is far better than orbital changes at shifting the whole planet's temperature. The gas moves between the oceans and the atmosphere as ocean circulation changes, which can be triggered by many things. Orbital cycles may set the timing, but carbon dioxide does the work of cooling the globe.

choices.text: show that the crater beneath Mexico is older than the iridium layer.
choices.rationale: The finding concerns the lava, not the crater's age.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 1's view that the impact was the main cause of the extinction.
choices.rationale: The timing of the lava says nothing against the impact; if anything it removes a rival explanation.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2's view that volcanic eruptions caused the extinction.
choices.rationale: Correct. If most eruptions came after the extinction, they could not have been its main cause.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2 needs the eruptions to precede and overlap the extinction; eruptions mostly afterward undercut that.

questions.prompt: Scientist 1's viewpoint would be most weakened by which of the following findings?

choices.text: Warm winters have become more frequent on the ridge.
choices.rationale: Warm winters are part of Scientist 1's account.

choices.text: Trees attacked by very large numbers of beetles die even when they are otherwise healthy and vigorous.
choices.rationale: Mass attacks overwhelming healthy trees is Scientist 1's claim.

choices.text: Beetle galleries are found beneath the bark of every dead pine.
choices.rationale: Galleries are Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: Ridge pines removed before beetles emerged were replaced by new deaths at the same rate the next year.
choices.rationale: Correct. If removing infested trees does not slow the deaths, the beetles are not controlling the outcome, contrary to Scientist 1's view and remedy.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's remedy follows from beetles being the cause; its failure undercuts that view.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

questions.prompt: Scientist 1 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the difference shrinks on holidays; Scientist 1 does not discuss it.

choices.text: The temperature difference is largest in winter, when heating systems run.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the difference is smallest in winter.

choices.text: Replacing pavement with vegetation would lower nighttime temperatures in the city.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says vegetation cools the air and recommends planting trees.

choices.text: Waste heat from vehicles and buildings is the main reason the city is warm at night.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's explanation.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1 attributes the warmth to materials and the loss of vegetation, so adding vegetation should help.

stimulus.title: The Warm City
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The city center is about 4°C warmer at night than the surrounding farmland because of what the city is made of. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and store the heat, releasing it slowly after sunset. These surfaces are also dark, so they reflect less sunlight than fields and forests do. Vegetation cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, but the city has replaced most plants with pavement. The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights, when stored heat is released most effectively, and smallest in winter, when the sun is weak. Painting roofs white and planting trees would reduce the difference.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The warmth comes mainly from the energy people use. Every engine, air conditioner, furnace, and light releases heat into the city's air. In the dense center, this waste heat per square kilometer can rival the energy delivered by sunlight. The nighttime difference is large because the city keeps releasing heat after the sun sets, while the countryside does not. The difference also grows on weekdays, when traffic and business activity are heaviest, and shrinks on holidays, something that building materials alone cannot explain. Reducing energy use and improving the efficiency of vehicles and buildings would do more than changing roof colors.

choices.text: weekday traffic is what drives the temperature difference.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 cites weekday traffic.

stimulus.title: The Collapse at Carver Road
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The sudden hole that opened beneath Carver Road formed because rainwater slowly dissolved the limestone beneath the surface. Limestone is made of a mineral that dissolves in slightly acidic water, and rain becomes acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil. Over thousands of years, water seeping down through cracks widened them into a cavern. The roof of the cavern thinned until it could no longer hold up the road. Caves and springs are common in the surrounding countryside, and the hole has sheer walls of solid limestone, exactly as expected when a cavern roof gives way.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The hole formed because a leaking water main washed away the soil beneath the road. The main, installed sixty years ago, runs directly under the collapse and was found to be cracked. Escaping water carried fine soil particles into a nearby storm drain, leaving a growing void just below the pavement. Limestone caverns take thousands of years to form, but the road showed no sign of sinking until two months before the collapse, soon after water pressure in the main was raised. The hole's walls are mostly loose soil, and the solid rock lies several meters deeper. Repairing the main is the key to preventing another collapse.

stimulus.title: The Bleaching Reef
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The reef bleached because the water became too warm. Corals live with tiny algae inside their tissues that supply most of their food and give them their color. When water temperature stays more than about one degree above the summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down: the coral expels the algae and turns white. Satellite records show that the sea surface over the reef was unusually warm for six weeks before the bleaching, and the most heavily bleached patches were in shallow water, where the water warmed most. Reefs far from any town or farm bleached in the same weeks, which only a regional cause such as temperature can explain.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The main cause was runoff from the land. Heavy rains in the months before the bleaching carried soil, fertilizer, and sewage from the coast onto the reef. Sediment clouds the water and settles on the corals, smothering them, while nutrients feed seaweeds that overgrow the coral and bacteria that attack its tissue. Water samples near the river mouth showed nutrient levels several times higher than normal, and bleaching was most severe on the parts of the reef closest to the river. Warm water can stress corals, but these corals had survived warmer summers before. The difference this year was the condition of the water, not its temperature alone.

questions.prompt: Scientist 1's viewpoint would be most weakened by which of the following findings?

choices.text: Sensors show the sway reached full strength before any pedestrian had stepped onto the deck.
choices.rationale: Correct. Motion that begins before anyone is on the bridge cannot be caused by walkers.

choices.text: Video shows the walkers widening their stance and stepping in time with the motion of the deck.
choices.rationale: Synchronized stepping is consistent with Scientist 1.

choices.text: The sway was never observed on days when fewer than fifty people were on the bridge at one time.
choices.rationale: Dependence on crowd size supports Scientist 1.

choices.text: The sway stopped shortly after the bridge was closed to pedestrians.
choices.rationale: Stopping when cleared supports Scientist 1.

questions.explanation: Scientist 1's cause is the crowd; sway before the crowd arrived contradicts it.

stimulus.title: The Swaying Footbridge
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The bridge swayed from side to side on its opening day because of the people walking on it. When a crowd walks across a flexible bridge, small sideways movements make people adjust their steps to keep their balance. Many walkers end up stepping in time with the sway, and their combined footsteps push the bridge at exactly the frequency at which it naturally rocks. The more the bridge moves, the more people fall into step, so the motion grows. The sway appeared only when the crowd was large and stopped within minutes when the crowd was cleared, and no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The sway was caused by wind. As wind flows past the bridge deck and cables, it sheds swirling eddies alternately from each side, producing a push that switches direction at a regular rate. If that rate matches a natural frequency of the bridge, the structure rocks in resonance. The opening day was breezy, and the deck's flat shape is well suited to shedding eddies. Pedestrians certainly felt the motion and reacted to it, but their steps were a response to the sway, not its cause. Adding fins to the deck to break up the eddies, rather than limiting the crowd, is the correct fix.

questions.prompt: With which of the following statements would Scientist 2 most likely agree?

choices.text: Flat-faced stones with parallel scratches indicate transport beneath moving ice.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 2 cites the scratched, flat-faced stones as evidence of dragging beneath ice.

choices.text: The unsorted bed beneath the pebbles was deposited by a slow-moving river.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says only ice can deposit such an unsorted mixture.

choices.text: Pebbles become well rounded only after long-distance transport in a river.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says pebbles can be rounded in meltwater streams over short distances.

questions.explanation: The scratched stones are one of Scientist 2's key pieces of evidence for ice.

stimulus.title: The Pebble Layer
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pebble layer exposed in the quarry wall was laid down by a fast-flowing river. The pebbles are well rounded, which happens when stones tumble against each other in moving water over long distances. They are sorted by size, with coarse pebbles at the bottom grading up to sand, exactly what a river deposits as its current slows. Many pebbles lie tilted in the same direction, the way a current stacks flat stones against the flow. The layer is also lens-shaped, thick in the middle and thinning to the sides, which matches the shape of a river channel cut into the older rock beneath it.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The layer was deposited by a glacier and the meltwater streams that flowed from it. Beneath the pebbles is a bed of unsorted material containing clay, sand, and boulders mixed together, a mixture that only ice can carry and drop in one place. Several of the larger stones have flat faces with parallel scratches, which form when stones are dragged along beneath moving ice. The pebbles above could have been rounded in meltwater streams at the glacier's edge, where sorting and tilting also occur over short distances. The region's climate records show it was cold enough for ice at the time, while river deposits need no such conditions.

stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: Winter colonies in intact forest patches survived a severe storm that killed most butterflies in thinned patches nearby.
choices.rationale: Correct. Survival that depends on forest condition during a storm is exactly Scientist 2's mechanism.

choices.text: Milkweed counts on farmland fell by more than half over the same years as the monarch decline.
choices.rationale: This supports Scientist 1's milkweed explanation.

choices.text: Regions with abundant milkweed saw monarch declines as steep as regions with little milkweed.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 3's argument against Scientist 1.

choices.text: Caterpillars raised on milkweed collected from treated fields died at twice the rate of those raised on untreated plants.
choices.rationale: This supports Scientist 3's insecticide explanation.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2's claim is that forest thinning raises winter mortality; a storm that kills butterflies only in thinned patches demonstrates it.

stimulus.title: The Missing Monarchs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Monarch butterflies have declined because the plants their caterpillars eat are disappearing. Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed, which once grew between rows of corn and soybeans across the continent. Since farms began planting crops that tolerate weed killers, milkweed has been sprayed out of millions of hectares of farmland. Surveys show milkweed on farmland has fallen by more than half, and the decline in monarchs tracks the loss closely. Fewer plants mean fewer eggs laid and fewer caterpillars surviving to migrate. Restoring milkweed along roadsides and field edges is the most direct way to rebuild the population.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The decline is driven by what happens in winter. Nearly the entire population spends the cold months clustered in a few mountain forests, where dense fir trees shelter them from frost and rain. Illegal logging has thinned those forests, and butterflies in thinned stands freeze during winter storms at several times the rate of those in intact forest. Counts of the winter colonies show the sharpest drops in years with storms following logging. Even with plenty of milkweed, a population that loses most of its adults each winter cannot recover. Protecting the winter forests must come first.

Scientist 3
Neither milkweed loss nor logging explains the full pattern. Monarch numbers fell fastest in regions where milkweed was still common, and some years with mild winters still produced small spring populations. The missing factor is insecticide. Seeds coated with long-lasting insecticides are now planted on most cornfields, and the chemicals spread into nearby milkweed. Caterpillars that eat treated milkweed grow slowly and die at higher rates, and adults exposed to the chemicals lay fewer eggs. The decline began within a few years of the coated seeds coming into wide use, which neither of the other explanations accounts for.

questions.prompt: Suppose a new analysis showed that the water-bearing minerals on Mars formed from water that was already present in the volcanic rock when it erupted, not from surface water. This finding would most likely:

choices.rationale: Correct. If the minerals did not absorb surface water, they cannot be where the rivers' water went.
The finding does not concern escape to space.
The finding removes the link between the minerals and the lost surface water.
The finding bears only on Scientist 2's reservoir.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2's reservoir only explains the missing rivers if the minerals absorbed surface water; the finding breaks that link.

stimulus.title: Where Mars's Water Went
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Mars once had rivers and lakes, and most of that water escaped to space. Early in its history Mars lost its global magnetic field, which had shielded the atmosphere from the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. Without that shield, the particles stripped gas from the top of the atmosphere, and the planet's weak gravity could not hold it back. As the air thinned, surface water boiled or froze, and water vapor rising into the upper atmosphere was broken apart by sunlight, with the light hydrogen escaping. A spacecraft orbiting Mars today still measures hydrogen and oxygen leaking away, and the ratio of heavy to light hydrogen in the remaining water shows that most of the original water is gone.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Most of the water never left; it is locked inside the crust. When water reacts with volcanic rock, it becomes part of the minerals that form, such as clays. Orbiting instruments have found such water-bearing minerals across large areas of the Martian surface, and rovers have measured water bound in the rocks they drill. Calculations of how much water those minerals can hold suggest that the crust could contain an ocean's worth. Escape to space is real but slow, and at the rates measured today it cannot account for the amount of water the early rivers required. Mars dried out mainly because its water was absorbed by the ground.

choices.text: whether coated seeds are planted on most cornfields.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not dispute how seeds are planted.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims is most consistent with Scientist 1's viewpoint?

choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's explanation.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 makes this claim.

choices.text: yellow pigments are present in leaves before autumn begins.

questions.explanation: Both allow that yellow is unmasked; the dispute is over red.

stimulus.title: The Colors of Autumn
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The red and yellow colors of autumn leaves are simply revealed, not made. Throughout summer a leaf is packed with green chlorophyll, which hides yellow and orange pigments that are present all along and help capture light. As days shorten, the tree stops repairing chlorophyll and breaks it down to recover its nitrogen, and the green fades. The yellow pigments remain and finally show. Red colors come from the breakdown of sugars trapped in the leaf once the tree seals off the leaf stem. The display is a side effect of recycling, which is why a leaf's color has no clear benefit to the tree.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Red autumn leaves are produced on purpose. The red pigments, called anthocyanins, are not present in summer; the leaf makes them fresh in autumn, using energy and sugar at a time when the tree is shutting down. Making them would be wasteful unless they did something useful. Anthocyanins absorb excess light and protect the leaf's cells while the tree pulls valuable nutrients out of the leaf before it drops. Leaves on the sunny side of a tree turn redder than shaded leaves, and trees growing in poor soil, which need to recover nutrients most, produce the reddest leaves. Yellow pigments may be unmasked, but red is manufactured.

questions.prompt: Suppose researchers removed all magnetite from a group of bees and found that, on sunny days, these bees returned to the hive from unfamiliar locations just as well as untreated bees. This finding would most likely:

Normal navigation on sunny days is what the sun-compass view predicts.

questions.explanation: Scientist 2 makes magnetite the key sensor; bees that navigate without it undercut that claim.

stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.
